identity.title: Functional Loss of Invasion Quantified in a CRISPR Knockout Hydrogel Model.

content.abstract: Genetic screens have transformed functional genomics but remain poorly suited for interrogating invasion phenotypes in defined three-dimensional (3D) microenvironments due to low nucleofection efficiencies and the lack of high-content, quantifiable invasion assays. Here we present a chemically defined hyaluronan-based hydrogel platform that enables quantitative, single-cell-resolved measurement of cell invasion and is compatible with arrayed CRISPR-Cas9 perturbation. Specifically, hyaluronan-oxime (HAox) was used to study the invasion of multiple patient-derived cell lines, modelling the invasive properties in two diseases - glioblastoma and lymphangioleiomyomatosis. Efficient CRISPR/Cas9 knockout of 93 genes allowed identification of potential invasion-suppressing targets, including effects detectable only at single-cell resolution. This framework expands functional genetic screening to complex invasion behaviours in controlled 3D microenvironments and may be broadly applicable to other heterogeneous disease models. STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE: Cellular invasion in cancer drives tumour recurrence and metastasis. Identification of target genes which correspond to a quantitative functional loss of invasion is challenging due to the lack of physiologically relevant microenvironments to model cell invasion in vitro, and robust nucleofection protocols to efficiently knock out target genes. We report HAox, a hyaluronan-based hydrogel platform, designed based on components enriched in the diseased cell microenvironment. HAox can robustly identify invasiveness of diseased cells compared to healthy controls in two model diseases characterized by diffuse cellular invasion. HAox, coupled with efficient electroporation protocols to perform targeted gene knockout, enabled efficient knockout of 93 genes and quantification of cellular invasion, providing a platform for researchers to perform high-content screening against invasion phenotypes.
